newsitem.title: UK: Moody's cautiously optimistic on East Europe banks.
newsitem.headline: Moody's cautiously optimistic on East Europe banks.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service said on Thursday the outlook for credit ratings of banks in Central and Eastern Europe is "cautiously optimistic".

The underlying economic positives, included the region's strong economic performance, moderating inflation, and good prospects for growing levels of foreign investment, Moody's vice president Larry Pellecchio said at a conference on bank credit risk in Eastern Europe.

"Among other positives, Pellecchio pointed to rapid progress the banks have made recently in recognizing problem loans and developing their organizations. He also expects that the region's banks will be likely to benefit from increasing integration between Western and Eastern Europe," Moody's said in a statement.
However, there were likely to be many bumps along the way to sustained improvement in credit quality, Pellecchio said.

Most notably, he cited "the current lack of complete legal and regulatory underpinings in Eastern European banking systems, the possibility of political policy reversals which could stifle economic growth, the incomplete state of enterprise restructuring, and the still incomplete development of commercial banking in the region."

Pellecchio said, trade flows between Central and Eastern Europe and the European Union have grown by more than 20 percent annually over the last five years, leading to a strong increase in investment opportunities.

"In addition, economic fundamentals are improving. Prices and wages are being liberalised, and trade tariffs are being phased out," said Moody's. "The reorientation of trade toward developed markets, along with local market restructuring, have helped to fuel GNP growth -- which is now ranging at between 2.0 percent to 7.0 percent annually for most countries in the region (with the exception of Russia), up from negative growth for nearly every country (with the exception of Poland) just four years ago."
Moody's said significant reductions in inflation rates in most countries (with the exception of Bulgaria) also boded well for the region's economies and banking systems.

Looking ahead, however, Pellecchio pointed to several major issues that remain to be addressed -- most notably, "fiscal discipline and social security reform, more complete privatisation and enterprise restructuring, along with continued financial sector development so that the systems are allocating credit more efficiently."

Privatisation represents an opportunity for banks in Eastern Europe to raise new capital and, where foreign investment is involved, to gain needed skills, Pellecchio said. In the long-run, privatisation is likely to have healthy implications for credit ratings.

But in the short-term, privatisation may have negative implications for certain banks if it means they will be less likely to benefit from state credit support. Privatisation also presents an important governance issue.
Pellecchio said many of the region's banking systems remain segmented and competition within systems is underdeveloped.
"State ownership without greater competitive incentive may encourage uneconomic business practices such as lending to nonviable state institutions and insider dealing and brokering," he said.
He added that "more complete commercialization of Eastern European banking systems cannot be achieved until privatisation advances further."

Pellecchio acknowledged that regulators in the region had made progress in establishing basic and progressively stricter bank prudential norms. Among areas which may not be up to standard yet and which were likely to bring some bank problems in the future, he cited the need for "better financial and market disclosure law, and insider dealing regulation."
Moody's currently rates more than 20 banks in the region, most of which have deposit ratings in the upper speculative-grade Ba rating categories.

Pellecchio concluded that over the next two years or so, Moody's could be looking at banking systems in Central and Eastern Europe, with average bank deposit ratings edging into the lower-investment grades.
